tldr: By wrapping an existing blind whole-body controller (WBC) with RECAL—a cross-attention layer between an environment point cloud and query points from the robot and held objects—the robot can cleverly avoid collisions and continue moving even when receiving imperfect commands that point directly into obstacles.
hero_caption: Overall system overview of RECAL. A single student model (RECAL), distilled from privileged teacher policies, corrects commands to a blind whole-body controller (WBC) online based on visual point clouds and proprioception. We demonstrate on a real Digit V3 that it automatically avoids collisions during confined-space carrying and reaching motions.
overview:
When humanoid robots perform tasks, whole-body controllers (WBCs) that balance the body while tracking end-effector and foot motions are widely used. However, most WBCs are "blind" and unaware of the surrounding scene geometry. If an imperfect target command that penetrates obstacles is sent due to teleoperation errors or rough planning, the robot faithfully tries to follow it, slamming its torso, arms, or carried objects into walls and shelves.

Rather than rebuilding a robust WBC from scratch, the authors took a clever approach: wrapping the existing WBC with a collision-avoidance layer. This layer is called RECAL (Robot–Environment Cross-Attention Layer). RECAL uses a cross-attention mechanism that queries an egocentric environment point cloud using the robot's joints and the bounding box vertices of held objects. This allows the system to directly and locally perceive which robot body parts or object corners are about to collide with which obstacles, modifying commands toward a safe direction only when danger arises.

By distilling privileged teachers (which have access to exact obstacle shapes) into a single student model in simulation, RECAL achieved collision-free success rates that far exceed conventional PointNet- or voxel-based encoders across diverse tasks such as walking, object carrying, and standing manipulation. Furthermore, on a real Digit V3 humanoid, they demonstrated that it corrects commands in real time using camera point clouds to avoid collisions.
contributions: Built a humanoid whole-body control framework that tracks floating-base (locomotion) and end-effector commands while simultaneously avoiding environmental collisions for the entire robot body and held objects.
Proposed RECAL, a geometric feature extraction layer that performs cross-attention between environment point clouds using robot body parts and held-object bounding box vertices as queries.

Achieved a real-time controller operating purely on vision and proprioception by distilling from privileged teachers (an analytical CBF-based teacher and a reinforcement learning teacher) into a single student model.
Demonstrated real-world loco-manipulation on a physical Digit V3 humanoid in addition to rigorous benchmark evaluations in simulation.

sections.heading: Why do humanoid robots collide with obstacles?
sections.summary: Many humanoid whole-body controllers (WBCs) are blind to their surroundings, leading to collisions when upstream commands are imperfect. This work proposes RECAL, a learning-based layer that wraps an existing WBC to resolve local geometric collisions.
sections.details:
In humanoid robot control, the whole-body controller (WBC) plays a central role by taking target trajectories from a planner or teleoperator and converting them into joint torques or PD targets while maintaining balance. However, in cluttered or tight indoor environments, upstream commands are not always collision-free. Due to sensor noise, coarse human teleoperation, or planner approximations, imperfect target motions that penetrate obstacles are commonplace.

Because most existing WBCs are blind to scene geometry, they try to track unreasonable commands as given, crashing the torso, arms, or carried items into nearby walls. It is impractical to always demand that upstream planners or operators provide a perfect trajectory where every single robot part remains completely collision-free.

The key insight here is a division of responsibility: upstream commands provide rough guidance, while the control layer handles local geometric collision avoidance. RECAL (Robot–Environment Cross-Attention Layer) realizes this paradigm. It acts as a learned wrapper layer that rewrites input commands for an existing, robust blind WBC into safe commands in real time.

captions.F1: Overall system workflow. On the left, two types of privileged teachers (for locomotion and reaching) are trained. In the middle, they are distilled into a single RECAL student model that takes only visual point clouds. As shown on the right, it is directly deployed to the real robot to safely adapt inputs to the WBC.

sections.heading: The limits of optimization and how to feed 3D shapes to a controller
sections.summary: Classical optimization-based control suffers from model discrepancies and high-dimensional computational costs, while recent deep RL has not unified collision avoidance across locomotion, end-effector tracking, and object carrying. RECAL tackles this with cross-attention using robot and object locations as queries.
sections.details:
### Classical and Optimization-Based Collision Avoidance
Classical methods such as artificial potential fields, operational space control (OSC), and prioritized whole-body optimization have been studied for decades. While highly interpretable, they require accurate geometric models, and online optimization costs surge drastically in high-dimensional, contact-rich, cluttered environments.

### Learning-Based Humanoid Control
Recently, deep RL-based WBCs have shown remarkable progress, but most are blind or specialized for blind terrain locomotion. While some works use proximity sensors or voxels to steer clear of obstacles, no prior learning-based WBC has unified floating-base locomotion, end-effector tracking, and collision avoidance for held objects.

### 3D Geometric Representations for Control
How to represent 3D environmental geometry is crucial. Global point cloud features like PointNet or voxel grids are great at summarizing entire scenes, but they struggle to directly capture fine-grained relational questions like "Which body part or object corner is close to which obstacle?" Therefore, this work uses robot joints and held-object bounding box vertices as "queries" to attend over the environment point cloud. This directly extracts critical local geometric relationships with low computational overhead.

sections.heading: Problem formulation: How to correct imperfect commands
sections.summary: The controller receives the robot state, an environment point cloud, held-object bounding boxes, and upstream target commands as inputs. The goal is to track targets as closely as possible while keeping unintended collisions of the body and objects at zero.
sections.details:
The robot's proprioceptive state is defined as $s_t = (\theta_t, \dot{\theta}_t, \alpha_t, q_t)$, where $\theta_t, \dot{\theta}_t$ are the joint angles and velocities of $J$ actuators, $\alpha_t$ is the base angular velocity, and $q_t$ is the base orientation quaternion. Environment geometry is captured as an egocentric point cloud $\mathcal{P}_t \subset \mathbb{R}^3$. Points corresponding to intended contact surfaces, such as under the feet, are pruned beforehand. The geometry of objects held by the hands is represented by bounding boxes $b_t^L, b_t^R$ tied to the left and right end-effectors; if nothing is held, box proxies for the hands themselves are used.

Upstream target commands are given as $c_t = (v_t, \omega_t, \eta_t, e_t^R, e_t^L, f_t)$, where $v_t$ is the base linear velocity, $\omega_t$ is the yaw rate, $\eta_t$ is the base orientation, and $e_t^R, e_t^L$ are the right and left end-effector positions in the base frame. A notable element is the binary flag $f_t \in \{0, 1\}$, which specifies whether end-effector poses should remain frozen during locomotion. For instance, when securely carrying an object, $f_t = 1$, so the controller keeps the arms fixed and avoids collisions purely by altering the leg locomotion path. Conversely, when $f_t = 0$, the robot can flexibly tuck its arms in to dodge obstacles.

The final output of the controller is the PD target angles $a_t$ for all $J$ joints. The objective is to follow the target command $c_t$ as closely as possible while avoiding unwanted contact with the environment and objects.

sections.heading: RECAL architecture: Placing a smart skin over a fixed foundation
sections.summary: An existing blind WBC (MHC) remains frozen, preceded by RECAL, which consists of a geometry encoder and a recurrent command adapter. Thirty-seven query points attend to the environment point cloud to safely modify commands.
sections.details:
### IV-A Base Whole-Body Controller (Base WBC)
This work does not train a base WBC from scratch. Instead, it freezes the Masked Humanoid Controller (MHC), whose Sim-to-Real transferability has been verified on the Digit V3 humanoid in prior work. MHC offers robust walking and balance maintenance, but it cannot see surrounding obstacles. Upon receiving an input command $\hat{c}_t$ (such as base velocities and arm joint targets), it outputs PD target positions for all 20 joints.

### IV-B RECAL Architecture
RECAL ($\pi^{\mathrm{REC}}$) converts the original command $c_t$ into a safe command $\hat{c}_t$ that the base WBC can track. It consists of a geometry encoder $E_\phi$ and a recurrent (LSTM) command adapter.

The geometry encoder takes the environment point cloud $\mathcal{P}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}$ and a set of $M=37$ query points $\mathcal{Q}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 3}$ representing the robot and held objects. The query points consist of:
- 13 body keypoints computed via forward kinematics (3 on the torso, 3 on each arm, and 4 on the knees and feet)
- 8 vertices of a two-handed held box
- 16 vertices from the bounding boxes of the left and right end-effectors (or single-hand held objects; 8 each)

Each query point is assigned an anatomical ID embedding and performs multi-head cross-attention over the environment point cloud features. This produces query-wise collision-risk features $Z_t$, answering questions like "Is a shelf edge near the right wrist?" or "Will the back-right corner of the carried box hit a wall?"

These features are compressed with an MLP, concatenated with proprioception $s_t$ and command $c_t$, and fed into a 2-layer LSTM (hidden size 256). The LSTM smooths command adaptations over time and compensates for partial point cloud dropouts caused by occlusions. Finally, a linear layer outputs the adapted command $\hat{c}_t$ and forwards it to the base WBC.

captions.F2: Detailed RECAL architecture. Cross-attention is computed between the environment point cloud and 37 robot/object query points. The resulting local features are fed into an LSTM alongside proprioception and input commands to produce corrected safe commands.

sections.heading: Training via teacher-student distillation: Moving from privileged cheating to autonomy
sections.summary: Two privileged teachers utilizing ground-truth simulator geometry (a CBF locomotion teacher and an RL reaching teacher) are distilled into a single student model (RECAL). Loss reweighting ensures critical, rare avoidance maneuvers are learned effectively.
sections.details:
### V-A Training Environments
Training is conducted in simulators like Isaac Gym. For locomotion scenarios, robots are placed in large arenas scattered with obstacles of varying sizes, randomizing the robot's spawn point, object presence, and the arm-freeze flag $f_t$. For reaching scenarios, robots stand in front of shelves and cabinets with randomized shelf counts, dividers, and widths. In both setups, upstream commands $c_t$ are intentionally directed through obstacles so that naive tracking guarantees collisions.

### V-B Privileged Teachers Design
Because full obstacle meshes are available inside the simulator, two privileged teachers are designed using this ground truth:
- **Locomotion & Carrying Teacher (Analytical CBF Teacher)**: A control barrier function (CBF)-style safety filter. It projects base linear velocities into safe directions using privileged obstacle geometry, expanding safety margins by the object volume when carrying items. When arms are unfreezed, damped least-squares inverse kinematics (IK) also pulls end-effector targets away from obstacles.
- **Standing Manipulation Teacher (RL Teacher)**: A recurrent policy trained with PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization). Observing detailed furniture shapes, hand-proximity raycasts, and contact signals, it outputs base height adjustments and arm target residuals to reach into tight shelves without collision.

### V-C Student Distillation
A single RECAL student policy is trained to imitate the adapted commands $\hat{c}^{\mathrm{tea}}_t$ produced by these two teachers using an outlier-robust Huber loss. A key technique here is loss reweighting: since aggressive avoidance maneuvers occur infrequently across the dataset, time steps where the teacher deviates significantly from the upstream command to avoid an obstacle are upweighted. This allows the student to master sharp avoidance maneuvers without degrading nominal tracking accuracy on straight paths.

sections.heading: Experimental results: Navigating tight gaps without hitting carried items
sections.summary: In simulation, RECAL outperformed blind WBC and PointNet/voxel baselines in collision-free success rate. Attention visualizations confirmed focus on high-risk body parts, and tests on a real Digit V3 demonstrated reliable avoidance.
sections.details:
### VI-A Baselines and Evaluation Protocol
RECAL was compared against a "Blind" baseline (no correction), the upper-bound "Teacher", "PointNet" using global point cloud features, and "Voxel" using voxel grids as seen in prior work. Evaluations covered five tasks—adaptive-arm locomotion, frozen-arm locomotion, box carrying, standing reaching, and object reaching—across three geometric difficulty levels (Easy, Medium, Hard).

Evaluation metrics were Collision-Free Success Rate (CF Success $\uparrow$), denoting runs completed without any unintended contact, and Command Deviation (Dev $\downarrow$), reflecting tracking error under safe conditions.

### VI-C & VI-D Locomotion, Carrying, and Reaching Performance
In locomotion and carrying tasks, Blind dropped to a CF of 0.38 at Medium difficulty, whereas RECAL achieved 0.93, closely matching the Teacher's 0.97. PointNet performed decently but plateaued at 0.65 on Hard adaptive-arm locomotion (RECAL reached 0.91), showing that global features struggle to handle tight, delicate maneuvers. Voxel lagged even further behind, despite training for more than 5x the steps of RECAL.

This gap widened during reaching tasks. Accessing narrow shelves requires the hand or object corners to come within millimeters of shelf boards. While PointNet's coarse scene summaries and Voxel's resolution limits caused frequent collisions, RECAL maintained high success rates because each query point independently sensed its clearance from obstacles.

### VI-E & VI-F Attention Visualizations and Impact Force Analysis
Visualizing cross-attention weights (Fig. F3) revealed that while attention rested on background sink tokens far from obstacles, it sharply shifted toward queries on the hands or box corners that were about to collide as obstacles neared.

Analyzing contact forces (Fig. F4) showed that while Blind suffered severe impacts to the torso and pelvis, RECAL virtually eliminated torso collisions, reducing unavoidable contacts to light arm grazes with extremely low contact forces.

### VI-G Demonstration on a Physical Digit V3 Humanoid
Egocentric point clouds were gathered via two Intel RealSense D455 depth cameras mounted on the chest and pelvis, running real-time RECAL inference on a GPU-equipped PC (NVIDIA RTX 5090). Even when a human teleoperator intentionally commanded the robot straight into a wall, the robot reliably steered around the obstacle and recovered its target heading once clear. Real-world transfer was verified across all five tasks.

captions.F3: Shifts in attention scores for left and right hand queries during locomotion. As the robot approaches obstacles, hand queries strongly attend (highlighted in red and blue) to point cloud regions on the wall that present collision risks.
captions.F4: Average collision forces across robot body parts on Hard tasks. The Blind WBC (left) experiences heavy impacts on the torso and pelvis, whereas RECAL (right) almost completely eliminates severe torso collisions, limiting impacts to minor arm contact.

sections.heading: Summary and limitations: What it can do, and what it cannot do yet
sections.summary: While RECAL is a powerful add-on for collision avoidance on existing WBCs, it assumes flat, static environments, cannot see outside the camera's field of view, and does not support purposeful contact.
sections.details:
RECAL leverages existing blind humanoid WBCs, successfully balancing collision avoidance and target tracking via cross-attention between visual point clouds and robot/object queries. However, the authors frankly note several important limitations:

- **Assumption of static, flat environments**: The current model assumes flat ground and stationary obstacles; addressing dynamic obstacles and uneven terrain remains future work.
- **Sensor field of view (blind spots)**: Because it relies on forward-facing depth cameras, it cannot detect obstacles overhead or behind the robot.
- **Lack of contact semantics**: Because all point clouds are treated geometrically as forbidden obstacles, it cannot reason about intentional, functional contacts, such as grabbing a handrail or pushing a door open.
- **Limited expressiveness of teacher policies**: The CBF and RL teachers do not fully cover advanced maneuvers like turning sideways to sidestep through narrow crevices, restricting the student's behavior accordingly.
- **No infeasibility signaling**: The controller lacks a mechanism to alert upstream planners when a situation is geometrically infeasible and collisions are physically unavoidable.

takeaways: Rather than rebuilding whole-body controllers, designing a hierarchical wrapper that adapts input commands to an existing blind WBC is remarkably practical for maintaining Sim-to-Real robustness.

Using robot joints and held-object bounding box vertices as queries to cross-attend over environment point clouds detects geometric interference far better than global encoders (PointNet) or spatial grids (Voxel).

Distilling distinct privileged teachers—such as analytical safety filters (CBFs) and reinforcement learning (RL)—into a single recurrent student network highlights the immense flexibility of imitation learning.
limitations: Obstacles outside the egocentric cameras' field of view (e.g., directly behind or above the robot) cannot be detected, leaving blind spots unaddressed.
Because all point clouds are treated as impassable obstacles, the method cannot be extended to tasks involving intentional contact, such as pushing objects or bracing against walls.
If the robot enters a physical dead end where collisions are unavoidable, the controller has no mechanism to halt or report an infeasibility error back to upstream systems.
